The Salem NY Plan Contents 01 Foundation Introduction 5 Salem at a Glance 9 02 Vision & Framework Vision & Goals 13 Future Land Use Map 19 03 Recommendations Small Business & Economic Development 23 Arts & Institutions 29 Housing 37 Infrastructure 41 Agriculture, Natural Resources, & Open Space 48 Recreation 52 04 Implementation Turning the Plan into Action 55 05 Appendices Appendix A: Review of Local & Regional Plans Appendix B: Community Profile Appendix C: Public Engagement Summaries • Community Survey Summary • Stakeholder Interview & Focus Group Summary • Public Workshop Summaries • Planning Committee Meeting Summaries Appendix D: Detailed Zoning Framework All appendices are provided as a combined online supplement available on the Town of Salem website. 3 4 Heritage and Horizons • 1.o Introduction 01 FOUNDATION • INTRODUCTION The Salem NY Plan • INTRODUCTION Introduction The Town of Salem Comprehensive Plan provides a roadmap for the next 10 to 20 years, guiding decisions about growth, reinvestment, public facilities, land use, and resource protection. Building on previous planning efforts and extensive community engagement, it establishes a shared vision and a set of goals, recommendations, and actions intended to help strengthen Salem while preserving the qualities residents value most. A Comprehensive Plan serves as the Town’s foundational policy document, guiding local decision-making and future actions by identifying community strengths, addressing challenges, and articulating residents’ collective vision for the future. More than simply a planning document, it provides a framework for managing growth and change in a manner that reflects community values and priorities. The Comprehensive Plan establishes the basis for future land use decisions, zoning updates, infrastructure investments, capital improvements, economic development initiatives, natural resource protection, and community development efforts. This plan embraces the key principles of effective comprehensive planning by taking a comprehensive approach to the many factors that influence community life; maintaining a long-range perspective while remaining flexible to changing conditions; focusing on broad policy direction rather than prescriptive regulations; recognizing the relationship between land use, infrastructure, economic vitality, environmental stewardship, and quality of life; and serving as the Town’s primary policy guide for future decision-making. Through this approach, the Salem Comprehensive Plan charts a path that honors the Town’s rich agricultural heritage, historic hamlets, scenic landscapes, and strong sense of community while preparing for future opportunities and challenges. 5 6 Heritage and Horizons Why Update the Comprehensive Plan? Salem’s previous Comprehensive Plan was adopted in 1997. Since then, the former Village of Salem was dissolved; the Town has completed major planning efforts for Main Street, pedestrian connections, and wastewater; and community needs related to housing, agriculture, infrastructure, climate resilience, recreation, and local services have continued to evolve. This update brings those efforts into a single policy framework and addresses priorities that have become more prominent since 1997, including housing choice and rehabilitation, hamlet reinvestment, agricultural viability, infrastructure capacity, flood resilience, and connections among Salem’s arts, cultural, and recreational assets. The Plan also reflects extensive input gathered through surveys, public workshops, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, and ongoing collaboration with the Comprehensive Plan Committee, ensuring that it represents the shared aspirations of Salem residents. The Community Planning Process Developing the Comprehensive Plan was a collaborative process involving residents, elected officials, farms, community organizations, businesses, and planning professionals.. The planning team paired analysis of existing conditions and previous planning documents with extensive public input collected through surveys, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, community workshops, and regular meetings with the Comprehensive Plan Committee. This combination of technical analysis and local experience was used to identify priorities, test ideas, and refine the recommendations in later chapters. Throughout the planning process, New York State’s Smart Growth Principles served as a guiding framework for evaluating existing conditions, engaging the public, developing the Vision and Goals, and preparing recommendations. This approach emphasizes directing investment toward existing community centers, protecting agricultural and natural resources, supporting housing and economic opportunity, strengthening infrastructure, and improving long-term community resilience. Comprehensive Plan Committee The Town of Salem established a Comprehensive Plan Committee to guide development of the Plan. The Committee included residents, local officials, business representatives, farmers, and other community members who provided guidance throughout the planning process. Committee members served as important liaisons between the planning team and the broader community by reviewing draft materials, identifying priorities, assisting with public engagement, and ensuring that recommendations reflected local values and community goals. Committee meetings were held every two to three months throughout the planning process, were publicized in the local media, on the project website, and e-mail announcements, and were open to the public to attend. Meeting summaries are included in Appendix C. Building on Previous Planning Efforts This Comprehensive Plan builds upon and synthesizes recommendations from previous Town, County, regional, and State planning efforts, including: • Salem Comprehensive Plan (1997) • Washington County Economic Development Strategic Plan (2007) • Salem Main Street Renaissance Plan (2017) • Washington County Agricultural and Farmland Protection Plan (2017) • Washington County Tourism Study (2017) • Washington County Housing Transitions: Needs Assessment and Supportive Housing Action Plan (2019) • Forward Together Economic Resiliency Plan (2021) • Salem Pedestrian Connections Plan (2022) • Rural Workforce Transportation Plan (2023) • Adirondack Gateway Safety Action Plan (2025) • Other applicable local laws, zoning updates, and planning initiatives completed since adoption of the previous Comprehensive Plan Together, these efforts provide an important foundation for this Comprehensive Plan while ensuring that recommendations remain coordinated with broader regional initiatives. The Salem NY Plan Planning Framework: Smart Growth Principles The Salem Comprehensive Plan was prepared with funding assistance from the New York State Department of State through the Environmental Protection Fund Smart Growth Comprehensive Planning Program. The planning process incorporated New York State’s Smart Growth Public Infrastructure Policy Act and Smart Growth Principles to guide development of the plan. Smart Growth is a planning approach that seeks to balance economic development, environmental stewardship, infrastructure investment, and community character while creating resilient communities that meet the needs of current and future generations. Rather than promoting growth for its own sake, Smart Growth encourages communities to build upon their existing assets, make efficient use of infrastructure, protect natural resources, and direct investment in ways that strengthen quality of life. For Salem, these principles reinforce many of the priorities identified by residents throughout this planning process, including preserving agricultural lands and scenic landscapes, supporting downtown revitalization, expanding housing opportunities, improving infrastructure, protecting natural resources, and maintaining the rural character that defines the community. New York State Smart Growth Principles This Comprehensive Plan was developed consistent with the following Smart Growth Principles established by New York State: 1. Allow for and encourage neighborhoods with a mix of uses, such as residential, commercial and community spaces. 2. Enable a diverse mix of housing types, providing opportunity and choice for people of all ages, abilities and incomes. 3. Prioritize infill and redevelopment of existing buildings to revitalize neighborhoods and downtowns, including areas around public transit. 4. Provide well-planned, equitable, and accessible public spaces for people of all ages and abilities. 5. Encourage compact neighborhood design and concentrated development around existing infrastructure. 6. Preserve open space, agricultural resources and natural resources. Land preservation directs development toward areas that are already developed, minimizing encroachment on open space and natural resources. 7. Prioritize transportation options that are safe and accessible for everyone, including pedestrians, cyclists and public transit users. 8. Promote climate resiliency and adaptation, preferably through nature-based solutions, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. 9. Build on unique traits to create an attractive and welcoming community with a strong sense of place. Each community has unique attributes, such as historic buildings, natural surroundings, local traditions, or small businesses. 10. Engage in an inclusive, collaborative public planning process that considers the needs and character of the community. Throughout this Comprehensive Plan, these principles are reflected in the vision, goals, recommendations, and implementation strategy. Collectively, they provide a framework for guiding future land use decisions, infrastructure investments, economic development initiatives, environmental stewardship, and community improvements in a manner that is consistent with Salem’s values and long-term aspirations. 7 Heritage and Horizons 8 Public Participation Community engagement was central to development of the Salem Comprehensive Plan. The Town employed a variety of outreach methods designed to ensure that residents, businesses, property owners, farmers, seasonal residents, and other stakeholders had multiple opportunities to participate throughout the planning process. These efforts generated valuable feedback that helped shape the community vision, goals, and recommendations. Public participation activities included: • Community Survey: An online and printed survey collected community input regarding priorities, challenges, opportunities, and future goals across a range of planning topics. • Stakeholder Interviews and Focus Groups: Interviews and focus group discussions were conducted with Town officials, community organizations, businesses, agricultural representatives, emergency service providers, educators, and other stakeholders to better understand local issues and opportunities. • Community Workshops: Public workshops invited residents to discuss community strengths, challenges, future vision, and draft recommendations. • Public Hearings: Public hearings before the Comprehensive Plan Committee and Town Board provided formal opportunities for residents to review and comment on the draft Comprehensive Plan prior to adoption. These activities were promoted through the project website, social media, local media outlets, email announcements, flyers, and other community outreach efforts. Summaries of public engagement activities and comments received throughout the planning process are included in Appendix C. The Salem NY Plan • INTRODUCTION Salem at a Glance Salem is a rural community shaped by working farms, historic hamlets, waterways and open lands, a strong arts and cultural community, and a long tradition of civic involvement. Located in eastern Washington County along the Vermont border, the Town has maintained a relatively stable population. That stability has helped preserve Salem’s while landscape and settlement pattern, but it also means that an aging housing stock, limited infrastructure, changing demographics, and the need to sustain local institutions and businesses are especially important to the Town’s future. The Community Profile and public engagement process point to a consistent set strengths to build upon and emerging challenges that warrant proactive planning. Agriculture remains one of Salem’s defining assets and continues to shape both its economy and landscape. Nearly three-quarters of the Town lies within New York State Certified Agricultural Districts, approximately one-third of the Town’s land area is actively used for agriculture, and Salem contains roughly one-fifth of all farms in Washington County. Working farms, open fields, forests, and scenic rural vistas contribute not only to the local economy, but also to the community character residents consistently identified as one of Salem’s greatest strengths. Protecting farmland, supporting farm viability, and minimizing conflicts between agricultural and non-agricultural land uses emerged as recurring themes throughout the planning process. 9 10 Heritage and Horizons The Town’s development pattern reflects its agricultural heritage. Most new development has occurred as dispersed rural residential growth along existing roadways, while the former Village of Salem and the Hamlet of Shushan remain the community’s historic population and service centers. These compact areas contain a mix of housing, businesses, civic uses, and community facilities that distinguish them from the surrounding countryside and make them the most appropriate locations for future reinvestment and growth. Existing infrastructure, walkable street networks, and concentrations of services provide opportunities to accommodate additional housing, support small businesses, encourage adaptive reuse of existing buildings, and strengthen downtown vitality while limiting pressure for scattered development in agricultural and environmentally sensitive areas. Housing emerged as one of Salem’s most significant longterm planning issues. More than half of the Town’s housing was constructed before 1940, new residential construction has been limited, and available choices are dominated by detached single-family homes. Residents identified needs for smaller homes, senior housing, accessory dwelling units, quality rental options, and attainable housing for families and workers. At the same time, rehabilitation costs, property condition, and limited wastewater capacity can make it difficult to reuse older buildings or add housing in the Salem Hamlet. New tools, including the Washington County Land Bank, create additional opportunities to address vacant, deteriorated, and underutilized properties while expanding the range of housing choices. Salem’s population has remained relatively stable over the long term but declined modestly between 2010 and 2020. The Town also has an older population profile and a substantial number of households with limited financial flexibility. These conditions are closely tied to the future of Salem Washington Academy, local businesses, volunteer organizations, and community services: attracting and retaining families helps sustain school enrollment and the local workforce, while housing, transportation, health, and social-service options influence whether older residents can remain in the community. Salem’s proximity to employment centers in Washington County, the Capital Region, and Vermont creates opportunities, but many residents must travel outside the Town for work and services. The Salem NY Plan Natural resources are equally central to Salem’s future. The Battenkill, White Creek, Beaver Brook, other streams, forests, wetlands, floodplains, productive agricultural soils, and scenic landscapes provide ecological, recreational, and economic value while contributing to the Town’s identity and quality of life. Updated FEMA flood mapping and the Town’s history of flooding reinforce the need to consider floodplain function, drainage, stream corridors, and climate resilience in land use and infrastructure decisions. Protecting these systems can reduce risk while supporting agriculture, recreation, tourism, water quality, and public health. Salem’s arts and cultural institutions are unusually prominent for a community of its size. Salem Art Works, the Historic Salem Courthouse, the Georgi Museum, the Shushan Covered Bridge Museum, Bancroft Public Library, local artists, and community events contribute to local identity, tourism, education, and year-round community life. These institutions also create opportunities for stronger coordination, shared programming, placemaking, and creative-economy development. Public engagement repeatedly described the combination of agriculture, arts, history, and neighbors helping neighbors as one of Salem’s most distinctive strengths. Infrastructure is a recurring constraint, as well as an opportunity. The Salem Hamlet has public water but no municipal wastewater system, and previous engineering studies conducted by the Town documented how small lots, aging or undersized septic systems, and water-use restrictions can constrain restaurants, other businesses, building reuse, and new housing. Cellular service gaps, aging electrical infrastructure and limited three-phase capacity, sidewalk gaps, rural transportation needs, 11 and flood-prone roads also affect households, farms, businesses, and emergency services. Addressing these constraints in coordination with land use and development priorities is central to the recommendations that follow. Taken together, these conditions point toward a strategy of reinvesting in Salem’s existing hamlets and institutions while sustaining the working landscape around them. The Plan emphasizes practical improvements that expand housing and economic opportunity, support agriculture and community services, strengthen infrastructure and resilience, and preserve the rural character residents value. A full Community Profile covering these and other topics in detail is included in Appendix B. 12 Heritage and Horizons • 1.o Introduction 02 Vision & FRAMEWORK • INTRODUCTION • INTRODUCTION Vision & Goals This chapter establishes the community’s aspirations for the next ten to twenty years. The vision, principles, and goals were developed through the community survey, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, and the first public workshop, then refined by the Committee. 14 Heritage and Horizons Vision A vision statement is the heart of a Comprehensive Plan. It expresses what Salem aspires to be, not just what it wants to do, but what kind of place it wants to remain and become over the next decade and beyond. This vision emerged directly from the voices of Salem residents, property owners, business owners, and community members who participated in surveys, public workshops, focus groups, and planning committee discussions throughout the planning process. The vision statement serves as the foundation for everything that follows in this plan. The goals, recommendations, and actions in later sections are designed to advance this vision. When future decisions arise, about land use, infrastructure investment, community programs, or zoning, this statement provides a shared reference point to evaluate whether a proposed direction is consistent with what Salem residents said they want.
